tools.name: list-entities
tools.description: Summarise what a workspace holds, and read its entities a page at a time, reading the files and writing nothing. With no `response_format` it answers with the summary alone — the total and a count per kind, one row per kind, so it grows with how many kinds a workspace declares and not with how many documents it holds. Send `response_format` detailed for the entity records themselves: kind, name, apiVersion, description, labels and source file, read verbatim from the document that declares it, bounded to `limit` records from `offset`, with `more_remaining` saying whether to ask again. Call this first in an unfamiliar workspace: it takes no subject, so it is how you obtain the names the other tools accept — describe, validate and build refuse a name they cannot resolve rather than answering empty — and the summary tells you how much there is before you ask for any of it. A document counts as an entity when it declares both a kind and a name and declares no apiVersion outside Aggrega's own, so YAML declaring no kind — a chart's values file, a configuration file — is skipped, and so is a document belonging to another project, such as a rendered Kubernetes manifest. Pair it with list-releases and join the two on kind, name and file. Send `release` (a Release path, as list-releases returns one) for the listing in that Release's terms: the Features the catalog directories the workspace configuration gives that Release declare, and no document under a catalog directory only other Releases read — so a workspace keeping variants of one entity side by side, one per Release, is listed with the variant that Release builds with. `unread_linked_dirs` and `unread_linked_files`, in both shapes, name each link the listing meets that leads out of the workspace — to a directory, which is not searched, and to a YAML file other than a Release the workspace configuration names, which is not read — so a document an editor shows behind one is not listed as the workspace's own. Where the workspace's own configuration file, or the CI-owned overlay beside it, is a link leading out of the workspace, the configuration is not read: `unread_linked_files` names that file, the listing is the workspace's own read with nothing configured, `release` is refused, and so is every other tool over that workspace.

release.description: Optional Release path. The listing is then given in that Release's terms: the Features its catalog directories declare, and every workspace document except those under a catalog directory only other Releases read. Absent, the listing is the workspace's own.

response_format.description: concise returns the summary alone: the total and a count per kind. detailed returns the entity records as well, one page of them. Defaults to concise, because what a workspace holds is not known to be small before it is asked for.

limit.description: How many entity records one detailed answer carries. Defaults to 50. It bounds the records, so it has no effect on the concise summary, which carries none.

offset.description: Which entity record the detailed answer starts at, counting from 0 in the order the listing reports. Continue a listing by sending the previous answer's offset plus its returned, while its more_remaining is true.

tools.name: list-releases
tools.description: Summarise the Releases a workspace holds, and read their paths a page at a time, reading the files and writing nothing. With no `response_format` it answers with the summary alone — the total and a count per top-level directory — so you learn how many there are and where they sit before asking for any. Send `response_format` detailed for the paths themselves, each relative to the workspace root — the coordinate list-entities reports a file under, so the two answers line up — bounded to `limit` paths from `offset`, with `more_remaining` saying whether to ask again. `lockfiles` maps each returned path to the path of that Release's lockfile, in the same coordinate: the file pull writes and build reads, so you never work out where it lives yourself. `unread_linked_dirs`, in both shapes, names each link the listing meets that leads to a directory outside the workspace: no such directory is searched, so a Release inside one is not listed even where an editor shows it under the link. `unread_linked_files`, in both shapes, names each link the listing meets that leads to a YAML file outside the workspace which the workspace configuration does not name as a Release: no such file is read, so a Release behind one is not listed; one the configuration names is read and listed. Where the workspace's own configuration file, or the CI-owned overlay beside it, is a link leading out of the workspace, the configuration is not read: `unread_linked_files` names that file, the listing is read with nothing configured, and every tool other than this one and list-entities is refused over that workspace. Membership is decided by the file's own kind header, never by its name: a Release named without a conventional prefix is included, and a file merely named like one is not. Call this when you need to name a Release and do not know which exist — build, describe and validate each require one named and none can enumerate for you. Feed a returned path straight to the `release` argument of describe or build.

response_format.description: concise returns the summary alone: the total and a count per top-level directory. detailed returns the Release paths as well, one page of them. Defaults to concise, because how many Releases a workspace holds is not known before it is asked for.

limit.description: How many Release paths one detailed answer carries. Defaults to 50. It bounds the paths, so it has no effect on the concise summary, which carries none.

offset.description: Which Release path the detailed answer starts at, counting from 0 in the order the listing reports. Continue a listing by sending the previous answer's offset plus its returned, while its more_remaining is true.

tools.name: validate
tools.description: Check correctness without rendering or writing anything, across four scopes that mirror the CLI. Pass exactly one scope selector. `release` <path> runs the closure-scoped semantic-validation pipeline over a Release: it resolves the Release's Manifest and Aggregate, computes the catalog closure, and runs the closure-scoped extends and schema-pillar gates, the resolve/topology/IR pipeline, the Recipe and FeatureRecipe assertions evaluated against the Release's values as a build evaluates them before it renders, and the resolution-completeness checks. `entity` <path> checks one catalog entity file: a value its kind requires that the file leaves empty is reported first, every one at once, as a placeholder still owed with what it takes; then every kind is schema-checked, a Component or Feature has its pillar structure checked, a Workload, FeatureRecipe or Plugin has its shape checked, and a Recipe is driven through the real compilation pipeline around a synthesized Aggregate, Manifest and Release so you see the isolated render summary. That synthesized build wires no connection and attaches no Feature, so a Recipe whose render stops while its templates read anything under .context.inject, .context.uses or .features is reported as not attempted rather than failed: valid, with no diagnostic, and the text naming those reads and the sentence the render stopped on. What decides it is what the Recipe reads, so a fault of its own beside such a read is set aside with it; a template that does not parse and a reference the render refuses still fail. An assertion that calls fail, the Recipe's own or one its Component declares, answers valid with no diagnostic and its failure in `notices`, closed by a sentence saying a Release must satisfy it before a build can pass: the synthesized Release sets none of a real Release's values, so the check cannot tell an assertion waiting on one from one that is broken, and a build still halts on it. Any other kind is refused, naming the kinds `entity` accepts and the scope that checks it instead. `entity` with `release` runs those same checks in that Release's terms: the entity's references — the Component a Recipe implements, a library a pillar refers to — resolve through the catalog directories the workspace configuration gives that Release rather than the workspace's own, and no closure is validated. `plugin` <path> validates a raw .wasm against its describe() self-report — pass `type` for a binary-only check, or `entity` (a Plugin entity path) to cross-check the binary against the entity's declared surface. `catalog` true checks the whole catalog: schema-pillar structure, library resolution, extends chains, OCI-location collisions, and provider input-kind capabilities — over the workspace's catalog directories, or, in a workspace whose configuration gives its Releases catalog directories of their own under workspace.releases, once for each Release over the directories that Release reads, the answer's `passes` saying which Releases each pass covered and what it found. Each scope dispatches to the same core the CLI validates with and returns whether the target is valid plus each diagnostic verbatim. The selectors are mutually exclusive: `type` needs `plugin`; `plugin` excludes `release`; `catalog` takes no other selector; and exactly one scope must be chosen, `entity` with `release` being the entity scope. For a diagnostic you do not understand, pass its text to explain-error. `response_format` chooses detailed or concise (release scope, with no `entity`). You did not start this server, so a diagnostic naming a place on its host names it relative to the workspace root where it lies inside the workspace, and reads (location withheld) where it does not; the catalog scope's `target` is the workspace root itself, and is absent and marked `target_withheld`.

release.description: Path to a Release YAML to validate over its resolved dependency closure. With entity, the Release whose catalog directories the entity's references resolve through instead; no closure is validated.

entity.description: Path to a single catalog entity file (Component, Feature, Recipe, FeatureRecipe, Workload, or Plugin) to schema- and shape-check. With release, it is checked in that Release's terms. When combined with plugin, this is instead the Plugin entity cross-checked against the binary.

plugin.description: Path to a raw .wasm to validate against its describe() self-report. Needs type for a binary-only check, or entity (a Plugin entity path) to cross-check against the entity's declared surface.

type.description: Plugin type for a binary-only plugin check, verified against the binary's self-reported type. When a Plugin entity supplies the type, omit it (a disagreeing value halts).

catalog.description: When true, validate the whole catalog: schema-pillar structure, library resolution, extends chains, OCI-location collisions, and provider input-kind capabilities. A workspace that gives its Releases catalog directories of their own is validated once for each Release, over the directories that Release reads.

response_format.description: detailed returns every diagnostic; concise returns the count and the first. Applies to the release scope with no entity; defaults to detailed.

tools.name: build
tools.description: Compile a Release into its rendered artifacts — returned in memory by default, and also written to `dist/` at the workspace root, where `aggrega build` writes them, when sent `write`. Without `write` the render writes no artifact to disk. Pass the Release path as `release` (absolute, or relative to the workspace). The tool runs the full compiler pipeline through the provider render step and returns the produced files by output-relative path. Use it to see exactly what a Release would emit before writing it, or to inspect one component's rendered output while authoring. In the detailed response format each file's rendered content is included; the concise format returns just the file paths. Sent `write`, the finished render is written through the same write `aggrega build` performs, and the answer names that directory as `output_dir` and lists the files written relative to it; that writes inside the workspace, so over HTTP it needs aggrega:workspace-write. A render failure comes back as actionable guidance rather than a partial write (route it through explain-error if needed): a refusal the compiler raises while compiling the Release reads in the compiler's words with every cause, and travels as a structured `refusal` entry naming the document it points at, the key there and that key's position, with each finding listed under `findings` where it joins several. `auto_pull` resolves the Release's dependencies into the lockfile first, which reaches a registry and writes.

release.description: Path to the Release YAML to build, absolute or relative to the workspace root.

response_format.description: detailed returns each rendered file's content; concise returns only the file paths. Defaults to detailed.

auto_pull.description: Resolve the Release's dependencies into the lockfile before rendering. Reaches a registry and writes the lockfile. Defaults to false. The workspace auto_pull setting turns the same step on for every build, and this adds to it rather than overriding it.

write.description: Write the rendered artifacts to dist/ at the workspace root, where aggrega build writes them, and name that directory and the files written in the answer. This writes inside the workspace, so over HTTP it needs aggrega:workspace-write. Default false: the artifacts are returned in memory and nothing is written.

tools.name: pull
tools.description: Resolve a Release's catalog and source dependencies into the local cache and write its lockfile — it changes your workspace and reaches the network. Pass the Release path as `release`. By default it reconciles: a recorded pin is honoured and fetched at that version, an unpinned reference is resolved fresh, a reference no longer reached is pruned, and an unchanged dependency set rewrites nothing. Call it when a build reports a drifted lockfile, or declines an external reference the lockfile does not pin — a build renders only from pins the workspace already carries, and this is what makes them exist. Pass `verify` to compare the recorded lockfile against the resolution that reconcile would perform now, honouring the same pins, without writing the lockfile, the plugin trust record or any entity.lock — which is how you detect drift. Pass `upgrade_targets` with entity URIs to re-resolve only those, holding every other pin; no argument re-resolves everything at once, because that discards the whole lockfile and a tool call has nobody to confirm it. A Recipe or FeatureRecipe the Release builds from a catalog directory must have its inputs' pins recorded in the entity.lock beside it, and by default a resolution over one whose lock does not refuses and names the pin tool; pass `pin_sources` to run that same step here instead.

release.description: Path to the Release YAML whose dependencies to resolve, absolute or relative to the workspace root.

verify.description: Compare the recorded lockfile against the resolution a reconcile would perform now, honouring the pins it records, without writing the lockfile, any entity.lock or the plugin trust record. Drift — a pin, or a signature the lockfile or the plugin trust record records that a reconcile would record, replace or clear — and a missing lockfile, are failures. Under the offline posture a recorded signature only its registry can confirm is not checked, and the diagnostics name each one. Cannot be combined with upgrade_targets or pin_sources.

upgrade_targets.description: Entity URIs to re-resolve, in the bare authored form (core/database, for example). Each named pin is dropped and re-resolved to the highest available version; all other pins and the recorded external inputs are held. Omit to reconcile instead. Cannot be combined with verify.

pin_sources.description: Run the entity author's pin step over the Recipes and FeatureRecipes the Release builds from a catalog directory, writing the entity.lock beside each, instead of refusing on one whose lock does not record its pins. Absent follows the workspace's pin_sources_at_pull setting; either value overrides it. Cannot be combined with verify, whichever value it carries.

tools.name: describe
tools.description: Describe an Aggrega subject in structured form, rendering nothing and writing nothing. Two modes: pass `name` to resolve a catalog entity of any kind by its type URI and get its fully-resolved definition (schema, uses-schema, provides, labels) with inheritance applied; or pass `release` (a Release path) to get its dependency closure — what a Release is built FROM, not its shape — the resolved Aggregate and Manifest identities plus every catalog entity and shared library it reaches, with resolved versions. Use `name` to understand a building block before wiring it into an Aggregate, and `release` to see what a Release depends on before building it. Pass both to resolve `name` in that Release's terms — through the catalog directories the workspace configuration gives that Release — which is how a name that several variants in one workspace declare, one per Release, resolves to the variant that Release builds with. `name` may instead be a registry reference, oci://<host>/<repository>:<tag> or @<digest>, which reads the entity exactly as it was published there — reaching that registry with the login the machine this server runs on holds for it, checking the bytes against the digest the artifact's own manifest records and against nothing else, and writing nothing; a reference takes no `release`. Over a listener, a reference is read only from a registry the served workspace is configured with — its default registry, or one listed under `registries` — and a reference to any other host is refused before that host is contacted. `response_format` shapes the `release` mode: detailed (every reference) or concise (identity and counts).

name.description: A catalog entity type URI (any kind) to resolve and describe, e.g. core/compute/api-server — or a registry reference, e.g. oci://hub.aggrega.ai/component/core/compute/api-server:1.0.0, to read the entity published there. With release, a type URI is resolved in that Release's terms; a registry reference takes no release.

release.description: A Release path. Alone, the Release whose dependency closure to report. With name, the Release whose catalog directories the name is resolved through instead.

response_format.description: detailed returns every closure reference; concise returns identity and counts. Release mode only; defaults to detailed.

tools.name: get-schema
tools.description: Return the canonical JSON Schema for an Aggrega entity or contract kind, read from the copy built into this binary, byte-identical to the distributed schema file, and writing nothing. Use it to learn the exact structure, required fields, and value constraints of a kind before authoring or validating one. Pass the lowercase-hyphenated kind token as `kind` — for example component, aggregate, release, manifest, recipe, ir, or wasm-provider. Pass `list: true` (with no kind) to enumerate every addressable kind first. An unknown kind returns the full valid set so you can correct a typo without a second call. This is the authoritative shape source; scaffold derives its starter skeletons from it.

kind.description: The lowercase-hyphenated schema kind token, e.g. component, aggregate, release, recipe, ir, wasm-provider. Required unless list is true.

list.description: When true, enumerate every addressable schema kind instead of returning one schema. Ignores kind.

tools.name: explain-error
tools.description: Expand a compiler diagnostic or error message into actionable guidance, writing nothing. Pass the exact diagnostic text a validate or build call returned as `message`, and optionally the entity kind it concerns as `kind`. The answer carries the diagnostic verbatim and a pointer to the language-reference page for that kind; where the diagnostic opens with a halting condition's short code, it also carries that condition and the published walk-through of the authoring fix. It does not guess at causes beyond what the diagnostic already states; the compiler's own message carries the remediation.

message.description: The diagnostic or error text to expand into guidance. Typically copied verbatim from a validate or build result.

kind.description: Optional entity kind the diagnostic concerns (release, aggregate, component, feature, recipe, featurerecipe, manifest, plugin). Selects the language-reference page the guidance points at.

tools.name: scaffold
tools.description: Generate a minimal starter skeleton for an Aggrega entity kind and return it as YAML, writing nothing. The skeleton is derived directly from that kind's JSON Schema so it always tracks the real contract: it carries exactly the required fields, with the fixed apiVersion and kind filled in and a placeholder for every other required value. Pass the kind token as `kind` (component, aggregate, release, recipe, manifest, feature, and so on) and, optionally, a `name` to seed metadata.name. Use it to start a new entity from a correct shape rather than from memory, then flesh out the placeholders and validate. Drafting needs no workspace. The same drafting is on the command line as `aggrega scaffold <kind> [name]`, which prints these exact bytes to standard output. Send `example` instead of `kind` to WRITE one of the documentation's runnable examples into a new directory of the workspace — `dir`, relative to the workspace root, or a directory named after the example there when `dir` is left out — and be answered with the files written, relative to that directory, the commands the example's page gives for building it, and the documentation version it was read from; send `list: true` alone to be answered with every example there is, each with its level and the first sentence of its page, writing nothing. The directory must not exist yet or must be empty: one holding anything is refused and left as it is. Over HTTP `dir` must lie inside the workspace this server serves; over standard input and output it is taken as named, as every path there is. The examples are read from the signed documentation bundle published for this server's version — or, where none is, the newest published before it — kept in the cache every project on the machine shares and verified against the workspace's signature policy before it is kept or read: a bundle that does not verify is refused, never used, offline only a cached copy is read, and a bundle carrying a link, or an entry that would land outside the directory, is refused with nothing written. Fields of two forms sent together are refused. The same is on the command line as `aggrega scaffold --example <name> [dir]` and `aggrega scaffold --example --list`.

kind.description: The entity kind to scaffold, as a lowercase-hyphenated schema token, e.g. component, aggregate, release, recipe, feature, manifest.

name.description: Optional value to seed metadata.name in the generated skeleton. Sent only with kind.

example.description: The runnable example to write into a new directory, by the name the list of examples gives it. Sent instead of kind.

list.description: When true, with no example, answer with every runnable example the documentation publishes, and write nothing.

dir.description: The new directory the example is written into, relative to the workspace root; it must not exist yet or must be empty. Defaults to a directory named after the example. Sent only with example.

tools.name: import
tools.description: Turn a foreign source description — a flow or a service definition exported by another tool — into draft Aggrega authoring files, WRITTEN into the workspace this server serves. Pass `source`, the file or the directory to convert. The importer plugin that advertises the source's format does the translation: it reads the source, drafts entities from it, and this writes what it produced, creating parent directories as needed. A directory — a chart or a project, say — is handed to the importer as exactly the files of it the importer's declared file patterns select, each named by its path inside the directory: an importer declaring no file patterns refuses a directory, and a link among the files it would read, or to a directory, that leads out of it is refused before anything is read. Send `output_dir` to name the directory the drafts go in, relative to the workspace root or absolute, as every path here is named; leave it out and they go beneath the workspace root, where the command writes them when it is given no --output-dir. Over HTTP it must lie inside the workspace this server serves: a value climbing out of it, an absolute location outside it, or one leading out of it through a link is refused naming `output_dir`, and nothing is read or written. Over standard input and output it is taken as named, as every path there is, a directory outside the workspace included, and what is written is held, with its links resolved, to the workspace — or, for a directory named outside it, to that directory — as the command holds what its --output-dir names, so a link leading out is refused with nothing written. The answer names the directory as `output_dir`, the one every drafted path is relative to, whether the file was written or handed back. The importer is one this workspace's catalog holds or one of the compiler's core importers, which serve their formats in every workspace; a format no importer advertises is refused naming the capability no plugin advertises. A core importer this server's machine does not hold yet is fetched by the first import that needs it, from the workspace's default registry with this machine's own login, held to the module the compiler's release publishes and verified as a pull verifies a plugin, then kept in the workspace's content cache, so later imports reach no registry; nothing in the call names a registry or carries a credential. Where it cannot be fetched, the call is refused naming the importer, its version and what puts it on the machine. The catalog an import reads is the workspace's catalog folders; where the workspace names none, it reads the catalog its default registry publishes as one signed snapshot, at catalog/snapshot. A snapshot is fetched once: its signature is verified under that registry's trust policy, and it is kept in the workspace's content cache and read there, held to its digest, with no registry asked for it again. Which snapshot an import reads: with `upgrade`, the newest; otherwise the one the record beside the drafts names, fetched by its digest when this machine does not hold it; otherwise the one the workspace last fetched as the newest; otherwise the newest. The record an import writes names the snapshot it read by its digest. Offline, a call that would have to fetch one is refused naming what to do; a registry that publishes no snapshot leaves the import with no catalog, with a warning saying so. A `plugins.importer` attachment whose `uri` names an importer advertising the format, by identity and version, runs that importer at that version whatever other importer advertises the format too, and hands it — and no other importer — its `with.sources` and `with.settings`; where several advertise the format and no single one is attached — a core importer and one of the catalog's among them — the call is refused naming them. Leave `format` out and the format is recognised by the signatures the importers declare — the syntax a source is read in, the file names it applies to and the paths its parsed tree carries — parsing through the parsers the importer reads the source with, the one this workspace's catalog holds for a syntax or the compiler's own for a syntax it holds none for, reading the file named, or of a directory only the files a signature's file patterns select, and no network: a source no signature matches is refused asking for `format` and naming the formats the importers advertise — or, for a directory, asking for one of its files sent on its own as `source` or a `format` whose importer declares file patterns, naming only those — and a source signatures of more than one format match is refused naming them, rather than guessed at. Send `target`, a provider capability such as compose or helm — the word a Recipe's spec.capability binds to — to have a Manifest drafted beside the importer's drafts as manifest.yaml: each component type and feature type the drafts need, the types of a catalog Aggregate the drafted one composes included, is mapped to the Recipe or feature recipe of that capability the workspace's catalog offers for it, by its capability-qualified name with no version — the one there is, or among several the one named after the type — and a type with none, or with several and none so named, is left unmapped with a warning naming it, so a build of the drafts stops naming each instance or attachment of it; a mapping an importer drafted itself is kept where the catalog offers it for that type and capability and dropped with a warning otherwise. The Manifest takes the drafted Release's name and version and the Release's spec.manifest is set to it, nothing else in the Release changing; a Release already naming a Manifest is left as it is. A `target` no Recipe in the catalog binds to is refused before the importer runs, naming it and the capabilities the catalog's Recipes bind to, and nothing is written. Send `dry_run` to be handed each drafted file's path and content instead, with nothing created: every other behaviour is the write's, the same importer over the same source reporting the same diagnostics, so a source the write would refuse is refused under it too. Every import that drafts anything also writes, beside its drafts, `.aggrega-import.json`, the record of what it wrote — the `target` it was sent, where it was sent one, the catalog snapshot it read, where it read one, each drafted file, and each key of a drafted Aggregate or Release at every depth, with a digest of its text, any other drafted file recorded whole — and `dry_run` hands it back among the drafts. A call whose drafts would be written over an Aggregate already in the output directory is refused, naming it, and nothing is written — under `dry_run` too — because an Aggregate is the document an author goes on editing once it is drafted; every other file already at a drafted path is written over. Send `sync` to bring what an earlier import drafted up to date with the source instead, changing only what the import wrote — with no `target`, for the target the record names, and with one, for that target, which the record then names: a part the source left alone stays as it is on disk, edited or not; a part it changed, dropped or gained is written anew, removed — a drafted file deleted whole — or added, where what is on disk is what the import last wrote; and everything else — a key an author added anywhere, a comment not written directly above a drafted key, a file the record does not list — stays byte for byte. The answer's `drift` lists each part brought up to date, or under `dry_run` each part that would be, empty when the drafts are in step. A sync that would change or remove what an author edited or added, or add a part where an author already wrote one, is refused naming each part and why, and nothing is written; so is a sync over an Aggregate no record lists, and one whose importer could not finish writes nothing. What the importer could not translate comes back as diagnostics, one per construct, and an import it could not finish still drafts what it could — read `halted` for that outcome and the diagnostics beside it for what stopped it. Values no source can hold — an application's image, an owner's email, a model the source does not name, the name of a Kubernetes Secret — are drafted as empty strings, and the import lists every value still empty where the drafted document's own schema, or the catalog schema of a Component, Feature or connection it declares, says one is supplied. They are answered from the answers file — the one `answers` names, relative to the workspace root or absolute as every path here is named, or without it the one the record beside the drafts names, or else `import-answers.yaml` beside the source file or inside the source directory — which holds, under each drafted file's path, the key path inside it and its answer, and the answers are written into the drafts; an answer for a key these drafts do not leave empty is kept in the file and not applied, so one answers file serves every target. A secret's answer is the name of where it comes from — a variable name, ${NAME}, or a Kubernetes Secret's name — and anything else is refused with nothing written. Nothing is ever asked here: every value still owed comes back in the answer's `owed` — the file, the `key` leading to it as a list, the `question` saying what it is, whether it is `sensitive`, and on a secret's value its `secret_advice` — and as a warning diagnostic naming the file, the key and what it is, the answers file is written with each owed key present and empty, and the call fails with one sentence naming how many values are owed and where; write them there, or send each back in `answered` with its `file`, its `key` and its `answer`, and call again with `sync`. A sent answer is judged, kept in the answers file and written into the drafts as one typed at the command's prompt is: a secret's answer that is not a name is neither kept nor written, its value staying owed with the reason as its `secret_advice`; a value the answers file already answers is answered from the file, and an empty answer, or one naming a value the drafts do not owe, is not applied. Under `dry_run` nothing is written, the answers file included, no sent answer is applied, and the owed values come back in `owed` and among the diagnostics without failing the call. Where the drafts include a Release, owe nothing and the importer finished, the import then pulls that Release's dependencies as the pull tool does, writing its lockfile, so validate and build work on the drafts at once; offline it pulls nothing and a diagnostic names the pull to run, and a pull that fails fails the call with the drafts written. The drafts are a starting point an author owns and goes on editing; whether what they say is admissible is what validate answers, not this. You did not start this server, so you are not told where its workspace sits on its host: the answer's workspace root is absent and marked as withheld, and so is `output_dir`, marked `output_dir_withheld`, where the drafts went to that root. A directory you named in `output_dir` is told back by its name relative to that root, the one your own paths are named against.

source.description: The file or directory to convert, relative to the workspace root or absolute. A directory is read into the files of it the importer's declared file patterns select, and no link inside it is followed out of it. Over HTTP it must lie inside the workspace this server serves.

format.description: The source format, named outright — for example langflow, flowise, n8n, mcp, compose, dify, crewai, langgraph, google-adk or agent-framework. Leave it out and the format is recognised by the signatures the importers declare, the workspace catalog's and the compiler's core importers' alike.

target.description: A provider capability, such as compose or helm — the word a Recipe's spec.capability binds to — to draft a Manifest for beside the importer's drafts, mapping each component type and feature type the drafts need to the Recipe or feature recipe of that capability the workspace's catalog offers for it — the one there is, or among several the one named after the type — and pointing the drafted Release at it. A capability no Recipe in the catalog binds to is refused before the importer runs. Leave it out and no Manifest is drafted, except under sync, which uses the target the earlier import was sent.

output_dir.description: The directory the drafts go in, relative to the workspace root or absolute. Leave it out and they go beneath the workspace root. Over HTTP it must lie inside the workspace this server serves; over standard input and output a directory outside the workspace is drafted into, and what is written beneath it is held to it.

dry_run.description: Do everything except write, and hand back each drafted file's path and content. Every other behaviour is the write's, so a source the write would refuse is refused under it too.

sync.description: Bring what an earlier import drafted up to date with the source, changing only what the import wrote, as the record beside the drafts lists it. The answer's drift names each part brought up to date, or under dry_run each part that would be.

upgrade.description: Where the workspace names no catalog folder, fetch the newest catalog snapshot its default registry publishes, verify it and import against it, holding it from then on in place of the one the workspace holds or the one the record beside the drafts names. It changes nothing where the workspace names a catalog folder, and is refused offline.

answers.description: The answers file the values the drafts leave empty that no source can hold are read from and written to, relative to the workspace root or absolute: under each drafted file's path, the key path inside it and its answer. Leave it out and the one the record beside the drafts names is used, or else import-answers.yaml beside the source file or inside the source directory. A secret's answer names where the secret comes from, never the secret itself.

answered.description: Answers for values an earlier call's owed listed, each naming the drafted file and the keys as owed named them. Each is judged, kept in the answers file and written into the drafts as an answer typed at the command's prompt is; a secret's answer that is not a name is neither kept nor written, and its value stays owed with the reason as its secret_advice. Send it with sync once the drafts are written. Under dry_run no answer sent is applied.

file.description: The drafted file the value is in, as owed names it.

key.description: The keys leading to the value, as owed names them.

answer.description: The answer. An empty one leaves the value owed.

tools.name: gen-catalog
tools.description: Generate Plugin catalog entities from Wasm guests, driving the compiler's own catalog-generation operation and writing the entities to disk under the directory you name. Each entity's contract fields are derived from the guest's self-report, and its identity and runtime limits come from an authored overlay, so a generated entity can never promise a capability the binary does not provide. Two modes: `from_embedded: true` generates an entity for every guest embedded in the compiler (the `overlay` is a directory of per-plugin overlays); or `plugin` names a single .wasm file to generate one entity for (the `overlay` is a single file). `output_dir` is the directory the entities are written under. Regenerating over unchanged inputs yields byte-identical files. Use it to keep Plugin catalog entities in sync with the guests they describe.

from_embedded.description: Generate an entity for every guest embedded in the compiler. The overlay is then a directory of per-plugin overlays. Mutually exclusive with plugin.

plugin.description: Path to a single .wasm guest to generate one entity for. The overlay is then a single overlay file. Mutually exclusive with from_embedded.

output_dir.description: Directory the generated Plugin entities are written under.

overlay.description: Authored overlay: a directory (with from_embedded) or a single file (with plugin).

tools.name: describe-capabilities
tools.description: Find the tools that serve the entity kind you are authoring, then load full definitions only for the ones you decide to call. Pass `kind` (an entity kind such as release, component, feature, recipe, plugin) for the working set for authoring that kind: every tool here declares the entity kinds it serves, so a narrowed answer is what those declarations say rather than a match on the words a description happens to use. With no arguments you get that same index over every tool this server announces to you — each one's name, a one-line purpose, the entity kinds it serves, and whether it writes, and no argument schemas, so the whole surface arrives in one readable answer. Pass `tools` naming one or more of them for those tools' full definitions, argument schemas included, and nothing else. It answers about this server's own tools and no others. Every tool the index names is one this server has; this tool reads definitions, it does not run them.

kind.description: Entity kind to narrow the index to, so it lists only the tools serving that kind. Cannot be combined with tools.

tools.description: Tool names, as the index reports them, to return complete definitions for. The result then carries exactly those tools and nothing else.

tools.name: lint
tools.description: Run the publishing-discipline linter over a catalog entity, or validate a Release's resolved dependency closure, driving the compiler's own lint operation and writing nothing. Two modes: pass `entity` (a catalog entity YAML path) to run the publishing rules — naming shape, category-matches-directory, annotation-prefix discipline, and the like — which report at warn severity over local content without consulting any registry; or pass `release` (a Release YAML path) to validate every catalog entity the Release reaches against its composed schemas. With `pre_publish` (entity mode only) the previous published version is fetched and the proposed version bump is verified against the schema-evolution classification, halting on a mismatch. `plugin` overrides the workspace-configured linter attachments with a filesystem path. The operation is offline-first: a missing artifact fails loudly rather than reaching for a network. Every result carries the findings as structured data beside the human summary — each finding's severity, the rule that produced it, its short code (the code printed at the head of its advisory row, which `aggrega explain` expands), its message and the entity file it concerns, plus counts by severity, in the same field vocabulary `aggrega lint --output json` emits. A finding from a rule Aggrega does not declare, one a linter of your own adds, carries no short code, as its row prints none. A finding carries a line and column only when the rule that produced it located the issue that precisely; otherwise the file alone locates it. Use it before publishing an entity, or to check a whole Release's dependencies in one pass. You did not start this server, so a finding's file is named relative to the workspace root, and one outside the workspace carries no file and is marked `file_withheld`; a place on the server's host named inside a message is named the same way, or reads (location withheld).

entity.description: Path to a catalog entity YAML to lint against the publishing-discipline rules. Mutually exclusive with release.

release.description: Path to a Release YAML to validate over its resolved dependency closure. Mutually exclusive with entity.

pre_publish.description: Fetch the previous published version and verify the proposed version bump against the schema-evolution classification. Only meaningful in entity mode.

plugin.description: Filesystem path to the publishing-linter .wasm artifact, run in place of the workspace-configured linter attachments. Only meaningful in entity mode.

tools.name: connection-at-position
tools.description: Report which connection's entry a position in an Aggregate or a Release falls inside, so you can ask about attaching to that connection without reading the document's structure yourself. Pass `file`, the document; `position`, a `line` and a `character` both counted from zero; and the `release` whose compiled graph records the connections — a connection exists only on a compiled graph, so the Release is required even for a position in the Aggregate. The answer is `graphNode` and `connection` — its `socket`, its `alias` and the `document` the position was read in — exactly the coordinates attach-candidates and attachment-container take, so pass them on unchanged; or, where the position is on no entry an attachment is written in, `noConnectionReason` saying why. A position anywhere inside an entry — on its alias, its target or its attachments — answers that entry's connection; a position on a socket's own key, above the entries under it, answers none. The entries are the ones the compiled graph records: a connection a component draws, at its alias-keyed entry in the document the component was authored in, and every per-edge entry the Release writes. IT DOES NOT READ MEANING: whether a key is a connection is never guessed from what it is called. Pass `position_encoding` to say which units `character` counts in; utf-16 when omitted. It ANSWERS AND STOPS: it writes nothing to any file.

file.description: The Aggregate or Release document the position is in, relative to the workspace root or absolute. It must lie inside the workspace.

position.description: The place in the document: a line and a character, both counted from zero.

character.description: The offset within the line, counted from zero, in the units position_encoding names.

position_encoding.description: Units the position's character offset is measured in. Defaults to utf-16, which is what a session takes when a client negotiates nothing.

release.description: Path to the Release whose compiled graph records the connections, absolute or relative to the workspace root.

tools.name: attach-candidates
tools.description: Report which Features may attach to a node: the Features whose declared applicability the node's labels satisfy, evaluated through the same label match a build performs — so what you offer is what the compiler would match. Address the node in exactly one of three ways. `node` names a workspace entity by its `metadata.name`. `graph_node` names a node on a compiled graph, alongside the `release` whose graph it is. `labels` supplies a label set outright and names nothing at all — it needs no coordinate, so pass the labels you already hold and skip the lookup; this is the form to reach for whenever you have them. The answer carries the labels the match was evaluated against and which of the three sets they came from — `declared` (what a document declares), `resolved` (a compiled graph node's finalised set, which is what a build evaluates) or `supplied` (yours, which nothing here vouches for) — so you can explain any candidate from the answer alone instead of re-deriving it, which is how your answer and the compiler's come apart. It ANSWERS AND STOPS: it creates no attachment, writes nothing to any file and proposes no text; composing and applying any edit that follows is yours. Candidates come from the workspace and the configured catalog directories — for a `graph_node`, only those its `release` reaches, so a Feature kept under a catalog directory only another Release reads is not offered; join each on kind, name and file against list-entities for anything more to display. A `node` or `graph_node` that does not resolve is refused rather than answered with an empty list, so a typo never reads as "nothing may attach here"; a `labels` call has no name to mistype, so an empty list there means what it says. To ask about one CONNECTION the `graph_node`'s component draws, add `connection` with its `socket` and `alias`: the answer then also carries `slots`, each slot that connection's socket declares — its `selector`, `required`, `inject`, `sensitive` and `description` — with the `candidates` that may fill it, which are the Features whose applicability the node's labels satisfy AND whose own labels the slot's selector admits, the two rules a build holds such an attachment to. Where no slot may be filled the list is empty and `noSlotReason` says why — `feature-created-connection`, `ad-hoc-socket` or `no-slot-declared` — so never read an empty `slots` as "nothing matched". `candidates` beside it keeps its meaning: what may attach to the node itself.

node.description: A workspace entity's metadata.name, as list-entities reports it. The match then runs over the labels that document declares.

graph_node.description: A node id on the compiled graph of a Release, as the graph keys it. Requires release. The match then runs over that node's finalised labels.

release.description: Path to the Release whose graph carries graph_node, absolute or relative to the workspace root. Meaningful only alongside graph_node.

labels.description: A label set to match against directly, naming no node. An empty object is a subject in its own right — a node carrying no labels — not an absent argument.

connection.description: One connection the graph_node's component draws, to answer for as well as for the node. Meaningful only alongside graph_node and release.

socket.description: The dependency socket the connection is wired through.

alias.description: The name the connection carries within its socket.

document.description: The document an attachment on the connection is written in. Accepted and not read here: the slots and the Features that may fill them are the same in either.

tools.name: connection-candidates
tools.description: Report what an entity may connect to: the dependency sockets it declares, and per socket the workspace Components whose declared labels satisfy the constraint that socket declares over its targets — evaluated through the same match a build performs. Pass `node`, the entity's `metadata.name`. THE TWO HALVES ARE NOT EQUALLY COMPLETE and the answer says which is which, so do not present them as one filtered list. The target half is complete: those are the components the same constraint admits during a build. The socket half is not and cannot be — an author may legitimately write a socket the catalog entity never declared — so the declared sockets are a helpful start rather than the set of legal names. Each socket therefore reports whether it is `declared` or `ad-hoc`, and the answer reports whether an undeclared socket is accepted on this entity at all: a Component's own dependency surface accepts one, a Feature's attachment surface does not. Pass `socket` to ask about a single socket by name, which is the only way to ask about one the entity does not declare. Unlike attach-candidates there is NO coordinate-free form here: this answers about a named entity and takes no label set. It ANSWERS AND STOPS: it creates no edge, writes nothing to any file and proposes no text; composing and applying any edit is yours. Join each target on kind, name and file against list-entities for anything more to display. A name that does not resolve is refused rather than answered with an empty socket list, so a typo never reads as an entity with nothing to offer.

node.description: The entity's metadata.name, as list-entities reports it.

socket.description: Optional single dependency socket to report. Omitted, every socket the entity declares is reported. Named, only that one — which is the only way to ask about a socket the entity does not declare.

tools.name: insertion-point
tools.description: Locate where a new entry under a named container belongs in an authored document, so you can apply an edit without parsing the file yourself. Pass `file` and `container` — the structural path from the document root to the container the entry goes inside, such as the components map, a component's features map, or a dependency socket. THE CONTAINER PATH IS YOURS TO SUPPLY: this reads the document's structure and never guesses where something belongs from what it is called, what type it carries or what it appears to mean, so you say which key, and it says where that key's entries go in THIS document. The answer is a zero-width `position`, the columns to indent at, the nesting step measured from the document's own indentation, and `missingContainerKeys` — the container keys the document does not have yet and that you must write before the entry, outermost first. `entryShape` reports whether the container holds a mapping or a sequence, and reports `unknown` where the container is not there yet or holds nothing, because the document has not said. Where `precededByLineBreak` is set, begin your text with a line break: the position sits at the end of the line the entry follows, which is in range whether or not the file ends in a newline and disturbs no byte already written. It ANSWERS AND STOPS: it writes nothing to any file, composes no entry text and applies no edit — that is yours. Pair it with attach-candidates or connection-candidates, which say WHAT may attach; this says WHERE it goes.

file.description: The document to locate a position in, relative to the workspace root or absolute. It must lie inside the workspace.

container.description: The structural path from the document root to the container the entry goes inside: each element a mapping key, or a sequence position written in decimal.

position_encoding.description: Units the reported character offset is measured in. Defaults to utf-16, which is what a session takes when a client negotiates nothing.

tools.name: attachment-container
tools.description: Report where a Feature attachment for a node belongs: which document it is written in, and the container inside that document the attachment goes in. Pass `graph_node` — a node id on a compiled graph, as the graph keys it — and the `release` whose graph it is. DO NOT ASSEMBLE THIS PATH YOURSELF: a node's id and the scope it sits in are each joined with the same separator, so from outside there is no way to tell a separator apart from a character in a name, and a path you composed would look right while naming a key nobody wrote. Ask for it. The answer's `container` is a list of segments, in the exact shape insertion-point takes, so pass `file` and `container` straight to insertion-point to learn where in that document's bytes the text goes. `file` is part of the answer rather than something you already know: a node contributed by a sub-aggregate was authored in that module's own document, not in the Aggregate the Release names. For an attachment on one CONNECTION the node's component draws, add `connection` with its `socket`, `alias` and `document` — `aggregate` or `release`, either of which may hold one: the answer is then that connection's own features container in that document. In the Release it is the per-edge entry under the Release's entry for the node, reported whether or not the Release writes that per-edge entry yet, so insertion-point names the keys still to write; a Release writing no entry for the node is refused. A connection the Release drew is refused in the Aggregate, which holds no entry for it, and one a Feature drew is refused in both, because nothing is attached to it. It ANSWERS AND STOPS: it creates no attachment, writes nothing to any file and composes no text — that is yours. Pair it with attach-candidates, which says WHAT may attach; this says WHICH CONTAINER it goes in, and insertion-point says WHERE in the file.

graph_node.description: A node id on the compiled graph of a Release, as the graph keys it. A node contributed by a sub-aggregate carries a qualified id.

release.description: Path to the Release whose graph carries graph_node, absolute or relative to the workspace root.

connection.description: One connection the graph_node's component draws, when the attachment is for that connection rather than for the node.

socket.description: The dependency socket the connection is wired through.

alias.description: The name the connection carries within its socket.

document.description: The document the attachment is written in.

tools.name: edit-document
tools.description: Apply one bounded structured edit to an authored document and write the document back, preserving every byte the edit does not touch. One call adds one entry under one container, or sets one scalar, and it can do nothing else: `edit` names which of a closed set to apply, and a name outside that set is refused rather than interpreted. THERE IS NO EDIT THAT DELETES, replaces a block an author already wrote, reorders anything, or writes bytes you supply verbatim — so this is not a file writer and cannot be used as one. Pass `file`, the document; `node`, the structural path from the document root as a list of segments, which is the same shape insertion-point takes and attachment-container answers in; `name`, the key the entry is written under; and `value`, what that entry carries, whose meaning follows from `edit` — the entity the entry requests, the node a connection points at, or the scalar a value is set to. `value` is a JSON value, so a number stays a number and a quoted digit stays text, and leaving it out sets nothing at all. `socket` is read where the edit wires a connection and ignored otherwise. THE NODE PATH IS YOURS TO SUPPLY: nothing here searches for a name, because a name appearing at two levels would leave this deciding which one you meant. The result has to be a document you could have typed, and that is what the write is gated on — the composed document is checked against its own kind's schema and reaches disk only if that passes, and a refused request leaves the file byte-for-byte as it was. An entry already there carrying what you asked for writes nothing; one carrying something else is refused rather than replaced. Send `dry_run` to be handed the edited document as `content` instead, with nothing created: every other behaviour is the write's, the schema gate included, so a request the write would refuse is refused under it too. Whether what you wire is semantically admissible — whether a socket is one the producer declares, whether a Feature's applicability is satisfied — is what validate answers, not this.

edit.description: Which bounded edit to apply. add-component adds a component instance under a components container; attach-feature attaches a Feature to the node you name; wire-edge wires a connection inside one of that node's sockets; set-value sets one value on that node.

file.description: The document to edit, relative to the workspace root or absolute. It must lie inside the workspace.

node.description: The structural path to the node the edit is about, from the document root, one element per segment. For add-component it names the components container itself, because the entry being added is the node; for the other three it names the node the edit is about and the container follows from the edit.

name.description: The key the new entry is written under: the component instance name, the attachment's name, the connection's alias, or the value's key.

value.description: What the entry carries, as a JSON value of its own type: a string, a number, a boolean or nothing. Its meaning follows from edit: the entity the entry requests, the node an edge points at, or the scalar a value is set to. A mapping or a sequence is refused, because writing a block is not one of these edits. Only set-value accepts a value that is not a non-empty string, and only there does omitting it carry nothing at all.

socket.description: The dependency socket a connection is wired inside. Required for wire-edge and ignored otherwise.

dry_run.description: Do everything except write, and hand back the edited document as content. The schema gate the write is conditioned on runs identically, so a request the write would refuse is refused under it too.

tools.name: cache-status
tools.description: Report what the on-disk caches hold, reading them and writing nothing. Returns one entry per cached element with its size and, where it has one, its content digest — so you can total, compare or select without parsing a table. Every size is reported twice: `size` as the byte count to calculate with, and `size_text` as the same quantity written in binary units to display, which is also the vocabulary the size-taking operations accept, so a quantity read here can be sent back unrewritten. Each class carries a `reach`: `workspace` for the artifact cache under this workspace's own cache directory, `machine` for the compiled-module, plugin-describe and documentation-bundle stores, which every project on this machine shares. Read `reach` before proposing any reclamation: removing a machine-wide element affects workspaces nobody in this conversation has named. `machine_wide_classes` names those classes directly. `provenance` names the plugin identities each recorded guest digest resolved for, marking a digest more than one identity shares — it is what gives a compiled module a name rather than an opaque key, and it is metadata rather than reclaimable content, so it is excluded from the totals. Without a resolvable workspace only the machine-wide classes are reported. Where the workspace's own configuration file, or the CI-owned overlay beside it, is a link leading out of the workspace, the call is refused naming the link: where that workspace's cache sits is what its configuration decides. You did not start this server, so you are not told where a plugin it loaded from a file sits on its host: that identity is null in its place in `provenance`, and its entry is marked `identities_withheld`. A compiled module's `note` naming one is absent and marked `note_withheld`, and its `digest` is still answered. An identity naming a registry reference or a Plugin entity is answered whole. A source artifact read from a repository on the server's host is listed without its `label`, marked `label_withheld`, with its `size` and `digest` still answered.

tools.name: registry-list
tools.description: Report the registries this workspace is configured to reach and the signature trust posture of each, reading configuration, writing nothing and contacting no registry. Returns each entry's host, optional alias, whether it is the default, its trust posture as discrete fields, and whether a credential for that host is present. The credential state reports presence only — never the credential, never its shape, and never whether the registry would accept it, which would take a network round trip. It is read from the machine-wide credential store, so it is the same answer in every workspace on this machine. Use it to find the host or alias other operations accept.

tools.name: search
tools.description: Search the local index of the configured registries for publishable entities, reading an offline snapshot, writing nothing and contacting no network. Use it to find what exists to depend on before naming a reference. Returns each match's URI, kind, version, description, category, labels and — for plugins — socket type and capabilities, as values rather than a table. The reported `version` is the one a resolution would take: a version whose retraction carries a signature this workspace trusts is excluded and named in `retracted`, so an entity whose every version is retracted is reported with no version rather than disappearing. `indexes` gives each searched registry's snapshot age and `stale` marks one worth refreshing; `missing_index_hosts` names configured registries with no local index yet, whose contents are therefore absent from this answer. Refreshing the snapshot is a separate operation that does reach the network.

query.description: Case-insensitive substring matched against each entity's name and description. Omit to match every indexed entity.

kinds.description: Entity kinds to match (component, feature, recipe, featurerecipe, workload, plugin). A record matching any one is kept. Case-insensitive.

selector.description: Label selector over the entity's catalog labels, which include its category (component.aggrega.ai/category=compute).

capabilities.description: Plugin capabilities to match. A record declaring any one is kept.

plugin_type.description: Plugin socket type to match, for example provider or governance. Exact match.

registry.description: Search only this registry, addressed by host or friendly alias. Omit to search every configured registry.

limit.description: Cap the number of results. Zero or absent means no cap.

include_retracted.description: Report the highest published version whatever its retraction status, instead of the version a resolution would take. The retracted versions are named either way.

tools.name: config-show
tools.description: Report the configuration in force for a workspace and which layer decided each setting, reading configuration and writing nothing. Returns one entry per setting with its effective value and the layer that determined it — a config file, an environment variable, a command-line flag, or the built-in defaults — plus the layers that contributed in precedence order, lowest first. A setting's `source` is spelled exactly as the matching entry in `layers`, so the two join directly, and a setting the defaults decided names no layer at all because the defaults are not a layer that contributed. Use it to tell a capability that is absent from one that is merely not configured here: whether a provider, an importer or a governance check is attached is a setting, and the two cases call for opposite next steps. A caller that did not launch this process is not told where anything sits on the host it runs on — every value naming a path, a directory or a file there is absent and marked `value_withheld`, and a layer that is a config file is marked `withheld` in place of its path. An absent value is always marked, so it reads as kept back rather than as nothing configured; a setting nobody set carries the empty value its shape renders as and no mark. `host_locations_withheld` says which of the two answers you are reading. A registry reference, a version, a digest, a capability and the name of an environment variable or a flag are not places on a host and are reported whole.

tools.name: plugin-list
tools.description: Report the plugins this server can resolve and each one's own describe() metadata, reading them and writing nothing. Two groups: the guests compiled into this binary, which resolve with no filesystem, cache or network access, and the workspace's configured bindings. With no `response_format` it answers with the summary alone — a count per group — so you learn how many there are before asking for any. Send `response_format` detailed for the records: each plugin's group, reference, where that reference was bound, its self-reported type, version, commit, served capabilities, rendered input kinds, boundary assembly and exports, its readiness where it has one, and whether it resolved, bounded to `limit` records from `offset` with `more_remaining` saying whether to ask again. Use it with the configuration reading to tell a capability that is absent from one that is attached but unusable: the configuration says what is attached, this says whether the attachment reaches a guest that resolves and describes. A plugin that fails is reported with its failure rather than dropped from the listing. A caller that did not launch this process is not told where anything sits on the host it runs on — a reference that is itself a filesystem path is absent and marked `uri_withheld`, and a failure's text is absent and marked `error_withheld`, because a resolution failure names the places that were tried. `resolved` and `readiness` are reported either way. A registry reference, a version, a commit, a digest, a capability and the config key a binding was written at are not places on a host and are reported whole.

response_format.description: concise returns the summary alone: a count per group. detailed returns the plugin records as well, one page of them. Defaults to concise, because how many plugins a workspace binds is not known before it is asked for.

limit.description: How many plugin records one detailed answer carries. Defaults to 50. It bounds the records, so it has no effect on the concise summary, which carries none.

offset.description: Which plugin record the detailed answer starts at, counting from 0 in the order the listing reports. Continue a listing by sending the previous answer's offset plus its returned, while its more_remaining is true.

tools.name: pin
tools.description: Write, into the lock file beside a Recipe or FeatureRecipe, the content pin for every input the entity reads from outside its own document — it writes inside your workspace and reaches the hosts the entity's sources name. That lock file is the entity.lock in the entity's own directory. Pass the entity document as `entity`, absolute or relative to the workspace root. It pins a remote source whose coordinates are written out in full, a file an artifacts entry imports, and each file of a local source, by its path beside the entity; a remote source whose coordinates come from a template is pinned per Release by the pull tool instead, so no Release is needed here. Pinning is the entity author's step: call it before an entity is consumed or published, and after changing one of its inputs, because a pull over an entity whose lock does not record its pins, or whose local source has had a file added, changed or removed since it was pinned, refuses and names this step. The entity file itself is never written, and re-running over unchanged inputs leaves the lock byte-identical. Set `dry_run` to get the lock it would write without writing it. The pull tool's `pin_sources` and the publish-entity tool's `pin_sources` run this same step and write the same bytes.

entity.description: Path to the Recipe or FeatureRecipe document to pin, absolute or relative to the workspace root.

dry_run.description: Resolve the entity's inputs and return the lock the step would write, writing nothing. The content cache still fills.

tools.name: publish-entity
tools.description: Publish a catalog entity to an OCI registry: it writes, and what it writes reaches beyond this machine — the bytes every consumer of that registry resolves, and a signature that cannot be recalled from anyone who has already fetched it. Pass the entity document as `entity`, absolute or relative to the workspace root; a Plugin entity also needs `plugin`, the executable published inside its manifest. The destination is `registry`, defaulting to the workspace's configured one. Set `dry_run` to compute the bundle and the digest a publication of it would land, and publish nothing. Signing follows the destination registry's policy unless `sign` says otherwise, and a registry that requires signatures refuses an unsigned publication whatever you send — there is no argument that bypasses that refusal. Keyless signing resolves an identity from `identity_token`, and refuses loudly when nothing carries one, because nothing here can prompt. Set `pin_sources` to run the entity author's pin step first — the pin tool's step, writing the entity.lock beside the entity inside your workspace so it is part of what is published; a publication that does not run the step refuses a Recipe or FeatureRecipe whose entity.lock is missing a pin, a dry run included. The result carries where the entity landed, the tag, the published digest — under `dry_run`, the digest a publication would land — whether it was signed, what the pin step did, and how far the call reached.

entity.description: Path to the entity document to publish, absolute or relative to the workspace root.

plugin.description: Path to the .wasm executable, required when the entity is a Plugin. Absolute or relative to the workspace root.

registry.description: Destination registry host. Defaults to the workspace's configured default registry.

dry_run.description: Compute the bundle and report what would be published, with the digest a publication would land, without contacting the registry.

sign.description: Sign the publication. Absent follows the destination registry's own policy. A registry that requires signatures refuses an unsigned publication regardless.

identity_token.description: Identity token value for keyless signing. When nothing carries one the publication refuses rather than prompting.

fulcio_url.description: Certificate authority endpoint for keyless signing. Absent uses the configured or public-good default.

rekor_url.description: Transparency log endpoint for keyless signing. Absent uses the configured or public-good default.

pin_sources.description: Run the entity author's pin step on the entity before bundling it, writing the entity.lock beside it inside the workspace. Absent follows the workspace's pin_sources_at_push setting; either value overrides it.

tools.name: publish-artifact
tools.description: Publish a standalone data artifact — a documentation bundle, or any opaque file — to an OCI registry: it writes, and what it writes reaches beyond this machine exactly as a catalog-entity publication does, because where the bytes land and what resolving that tag returns are just as public. Pass the file as `file`, absolute or relative to the workspace root, with `name` and `tag` naming what it is published as. The bytes are opaque — no entity envelope is parsed — and `media_type` defaults to the documentation-bundle type. Set `dry_run` to compute the bundle and contact nothing. It signs nothing: a published artifact is signed afterwards by reference with the sign-artifacts tool, which needs only the reference this result reports. The result carries where the artifact landed, its published digest, and how far the call reached.

file.description: Path to the file to publish, absolute or relative to the workspace root. Its bytes are published verbatim.

name.description: The artifact name it is published under.

tag.description: The version tag it is published under.

media_type.description: Media type the opaque bytes are published under. Defaults to the documentation-bundle media type.

registry.description: Destination registry host. Defaults to the workspace's configured default registry.

dry_run.description: Compute the bundle and report what would be published without contacting the registry.

tools.name: sign-artifacts
tools.description: Sign already-published artifacts and attach each signature to the registry: it writes beyond this machine, and a signature is the one thing here that cannot be taken back at all — the artifact it vouches for is untouched, but anyone who fetches that artifact afterwards fetches the signature with it. Pass the already-published references as `references`; each is a registry address rather than a path. One authentication serves the whole batch, resolved before any reference is signed, so a batch with no usable credential refuses at the start rather than partway through. Every reference in one call is signed with one credential, so references whose registries the configuration gives different signing keys, or a key for one and none for another, are refused before anything is signed: send one call per credential. Keyless signing takes its identity from `identity_token`, and refuses loudly when nothing carries one, because nothing here can prompt. Signing a reference nothing published is refused rather than attached to nothing. `jobs` signs that many references at once; each is still signed exactly as it would be alone, and absent it signs one after another. The result names every reference signed with the digest its signature commits to, in the order the references were given.

references.description: The already-published references to sign, each a registry address (registry.example/component/core/api-server:1.0.0, for example).

identity_token.description: Identity token value for keyless signing. When nothing carries one the batch refuses rather than prompting.

fulcio_url.description: Certificate authority endpoint for keyless signing. Absent uses the configured or public-good default.

rekor_url.description: Transparency log endpoint for keyless signing. Absent uses the configured or public-good default.

timestamp_url.description: Timestamp authority endpoint for keyless signing. Absent uses the configured one; none is used by default.

jobs.description: How many references are signed at once. Absent signs one after another. Each reference is still signed exactly as it would be alone — when keyless, with its own certificate and its own transparency-log entry — and the result keeps the order the references were given.

tools.name: deprecate-artifact
tools.description: Attach a signed deprecation marker to an already-published artifact: it writes beyond this machine, and it is the sharpest of these to read wrongly — the artifact it withdraws is untouched, but every consumer resolving that reference afterwards sees the withdrawal, and a retraction a workspace trusts takes the version out of what a resolution will choose. Send either `reference` with `severity` and `reason`, or `from` naming a batch file, absolute or relative to the workspace root — not both. The content is required rather than prompted for, because nothing here can ask. The marker is signed by its own digest, so it carries the same irrevocability a signature does: keyless signing takes its identity from `identity_token`, and refuses loudly when nothing carries one. Every marker of one batch file is signed with one credential, so entries whose registries need different credentials are refused before any marker is attached: send one batch per credential. A marker against a reference nothing published is refused rather than attached. The result names every marker attached with its own digest.

reference.description: The already-published reference to withdraw, a registry address rather than a path. Mutually exclusive with from.

severity.description: How strongly the withdrawal binds a consumer. Required alongside reference.

reason.description: Why the artifact is withdrawn. Required alongside reference.

replacement.description: Optional reference consumers should move to instead.

message.description: Optional additional text carried on the marker.

from.description: Path to a batch file of deprecation entries, absolute or relative to the workspace root. Mutually exclusive with reference.

identity_token.description: Identity token value for keyless signing. When nothing carries one the marking refuses rather than prompting.
